name: Gadusol

lead: Gadusol is a small molecule that fish eggs and some other animals carry to absorb sunlight. It is related to the mycosporine-like amino acids made by algae and corals.
Researchers have proposed it as a natural sunscreen ingredient and have engineered microbes to produce it.

paras: Its conjugated ring structure absorbs UV radiation, and it also has antioxidant activity measured in fish-roe extracts.
No human safety or efficacy studies were found. It is not an established commercial sunscreen filter.

lead: Gadusol is a small natural UV-absorbing compound (C8H12O6), a substituted cyclohexenone, found in the eggs of fish and in some other vertebrates and invertebrates.[1][2] It was isolated from cod roe, where it occurs at about 4 g per kg dry weight, and its structure was confirmed by synthesis in 1981.[3] It is related to the mycosporine-like amino acids that organisms in high-sunlight environments use as natural sunscreens.[1]

Because it absorbs UV and has antioxidant properties, gadusol has been proposed as a sunscreen or cosmetic ingredient and has been studied computationally, photophysically and in bioengineered production systems.[2][4][5] No human trials of gadusol as a topical product were found.
infobox: Fish roe, other marine vertebrates and invertebrates[1][3]

paras: A 1981 study isolated gadusol from cod ovaries and found similar concentrations in other marine teleosts.[3] A 2015 eLife paper reported that zebrafish and other vertebrates can synthesise gadusol de novo, overturning the assumption that it comes from diet or symbionts.[6] Wikipedia notes it is produced by marine vertebrates and invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles and birds, and cites a 2023 study describing it as a maternally provided sunscreen protecting fish embryos from DNA damage.[1]

Gadusol absorbs UV through its conjugated ring.[1] Computational work assessed its photoprotective potential,[5] a photophysics study examined its excited-state behaviour and reductive quenching,[4] and antioxidant activity has been measured in extracts of fish roes from the Argentine Sea.[7]

A 2020 review of marine cosmetics identifies mycosporine-like amino acids and gadusol as candidates in topical photoprotection.[2] A 2019 study described combining genes from different kingdoms in microbes to produce novel sunscreen compounds.[8]
No studies found. Available research is limited to isolation, biochemical, computational and microbial-production work.
